events.excerpt: Application issue: Grant Application - Shielded Zcash Payments in KOKOPAI · Issue #556 · ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants · GitHub Summary. Integrating shielded Zcash as a payment system in KOKOPAI, an AI-created video platform with a marketplace for digital collectibles. Users add credits by paying shielded ZEC from their own wallet, and spend the credits in the marketplace. Requested: USD 14,500 · Category: Integration · Startup funding: none How it works. Everything on KOKOPAI is priced in acredits. On the Add credits page a user picks an amount, chooses Zcash and scans a ZIP-321 QR. KOKOPAI’s server detects the payment with a viewing key, verifies amount, memo, expiry and confirmations, and adds the credits. No Zcash spending key is on the server and no Zcash key is in the browser. Milestones # Deliverable USD Date 1 Zcash payment core on testnet: quote, ZIP-321, verification, example app, CI with a real testnet payment 4,950 2027-01-15 2 Zcash integrated into KOKOPAI on testnet: add credits, status, wallet activity 3,850 2027-02-05 3 Mainnet launch with real ZEC, security document 4,050 2027-02-26 4 Three months of maintenance and a usage report 1,650 2027-05-28 Open source. KOKOPAI’s repository is private, so the Zcash payment module is published separately under MIT, with tests and an example app. About me. I built zcash-faucet and zcash-testnet-wallet (both MIT, on npm) and have open PRs on zcash-devtool and sapling-crypto. Everything is listed at GitHub - anukulpandey/zcash-pow: Proof of work: my Zcash tools, contributions and posts, with links · GitHub .

events.excerpt: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. events.excerpt: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole. events.excerpt: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine.
